content: The systematic review aimed to evaluate and synthesize data on the effectiveness of breastfeeding promotion interventions in HIV-positive women on antiretroviral therapy (ART) living in resource-limited settings where exclusive breastfeeding is promoted due to the lack of safe alternatives for replacement feeding. The review was conducted by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. Research Question The primary research question was: In HIV-positive women on ART living in developing countries, what is the effectiveness of breastfeeding promotion interventions compared to no interventions in terms of initiation of breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding at 3 and 6 months? Methods The review included studies without restrictions on study design. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized clinical trials, and cohort studies that provided data on early breastfeeding initiation (within one hour of birth), breastfeeding initiation, and exclusive breastfeeding at any time point were included. Studies not published in English were excluded. Participants and Interventions The participants were HIV-positive women on ART, both preand post-gestational. The interventions included group counseling, individual counseling sessions, staff training, community support, workplace and policy support, and prenatal and postnatal education and counseling. Outcomes Measured The primary outcomes assessed were: 1. Exclusive breastfeeding at 3 and 6 months. 2. Initiation of breastfeeding. 3. Early initiation of breastfeeding (within one hour of birth). Search Strategy An extensive electronic search was conducted using databases such as PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, EMBASE, and others. Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by multiple reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer. Articles were categorized as review articles, qualitative studies, descriptive studies, or clinical trials. Full texts of selected studies were reviewed, and a final list of included articles was developed. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Data were extracted using a standardized online tool, including study design, purpose, inclusion/exclusion criteria, country, blinding, funding, sample size, dropout rates, participant demographics, interventions, and outcomes measured. The quality of studies was assessed using the Cochrane Handbook for RCTs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. Risk of bias was evaluated based on factors such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, and handling of incomplete data. Results Initial Screening: 859 citations were identified, of which 71 met the inclusion criteria. After further review, 13 studies were included in the systematic review. Study Characteristics: The included studies consisted of one RCT, seven cohort studies, four cross-sectional studies, and one pre-post study. These studies were conducted in countries such as Zimbabwe, South Africa, India, Kenya, Uganda, Malawi, Tanzania, and Cameroon. Key Findings 1. Exclusive Breastfeeding at 6 Months: One cohort study (Piwoz et al., 2007) showed higher rates of exclusive breastfeeding in the intervention group compared to the control group. Another study (Matovu et al., 2008) demonstrated a dose-response relationship, where more counseling visits led to higher exclusive breastfeeding rates. Three other studies lacked comparison groups and contributed limited evidence. 2. Exclusive Breastfeeding at 3 Months: The RCT (Tomlinson et al., 2014) showed a significant benefit, with 24% of women in the intervention group exclusively breastfeeding at 3 months compared to 16% in the control group. Each additional visit with a community health worker increased exclusive breastfeeding rates by 6%. Four cohort studies also indicated benefits, with two showing statistically significant results. Interventions combining individual and group counseling had a greater impact. 3. Early Initiation of Breastfeeding (Within 1 Hour): The RCT (Tomlinson et al., 2014) found no difference between intervention and control groups. A pre-post study (Mazia et al., 2009) showed an increase in early initiation rates from 24% pre-intervention to 33% post-intervention. Two cross-sectional studies reported early initiation rates of 50-80%, but these lacked comparison groups. 4. Breastfeeding Initiation: The RCT (Tomlinson et al., 2014) found no effect of breastfeeding promotion on initiation rates. A pre-post study (Mazia et al., 2009) showed an increase in initiation rates from 33% to 74% post-intervention. Other studies reported initiation rates ranging from 53% to 95%, but these lacked control groups. Discussion The review highlighted the impact of breastfeeding promotion interventions on HIV-positive women receiving ART. Strengths of the review included an extensive search strategy, in-depth quality assessment, and consideration of study design in interpreting findings. However, limitations included potential publication bias, the predominance of observational studies, and methodological issues such as indirectness and lack of stratification by HIV status in some studies. The RCT provided moderate to high-quality evidence, demonstrating that breastfeeding promotion increased exclusive breastfeeding rates at 3 months and showed a dose-response relationship with the number of intervention visits. Observational studies supported these findings, indicating that breastfeeding promotion influenced exclusive breastfeeding rates and reduced postnatal transmission. Limitations The quality of observational studies ranged from poor to fair, with methodological issues such as indirectness and sample bias. The lack of control groups in many studies limited the strength of the evidence. Conclusion Breastfeeding promotion interventions, particularly those involving frequent and combined individual and group counseling, were effective in increasing exclusive breastfeeding rates among HIV-positive women on ART. However, further high-quality RCTs are needed to strengthen the evidence base.
